clue.text: Her BBC cameo involved a white Roller

indicators.note: something involved is tangled and complicated, so the preceding letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: eleven letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An actress makes a brief BBC appearance that somehow involves a white Rolls-Royce.
explanation.walkthrough: Roller looks like slang for a Rolls-Royce car, but here it is a wave; a beachcomber is a long wave that rolls in and breaks white on the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides a scavenger on the shore, the word names a long curling breaker sweeping in from the sea onto a beach.

clue.text: Cheese produced that's revolting

indicators.note: revolting is read as turning over or rolling back, so the word before it runs the other way

parts.note: produced means made

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the cheese they have been given is disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' poses as disgusting, a natural thing to say about a cheese, but it means turning round.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is a mild Dutch cheese sold in balls with red wax rind, an example of the category.

clue.text: Astute chap who tried to stop 1s has article spiked

indicators.note: to spike something is to kill it off or stop it running, so the article is struck out of the name

parts.note: King Canute is said to have ordered the incoming waves to stop; 1s refers to the answer at 1-across, rolling waves
an indefinite article

explanation.surface: A clever man who once tried to hold back the tide has a newspaper piece of his rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 1s means waves, pointing to the legend of Canute on the seashore; taking AN out of CANUTE leaves CUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Cute in its older sense means shrewd or sharp-witted, like the clipped form of acute it came from.

clue.text: Dramatist to get on with to-do list, we're told?

indicators.note: what we are told is heard rather than read, so the phrase is matched by its sound

parts.words: to get on with to-do list
parts.note: working through a to-do list means ticking items off one by one

explanation.surface: A playwright resolves to get stuck into a list of chores.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken aloud, the Russian playwright's surname sounds like 'check off'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anton Chekhov wrote The Seagull and The Cherry Orchard, so he is a famous example of a playwright.

clue.text: Low resistance fell

parts.note: to low is to make the sound a cow makes
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Weak opposition collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word changes job: 'Low' is a cow's call, not weak, and 'fell' is a noun for hill country, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A fell is an upland stretch of open hillside in northern England, much the same as a moor or heath.

clue.text: Welshman starts to gild English language gospel

parts.note: Evan is a typical Welsh first name

indicators.note: starts points at the opening letter of each of the following words

parts.note: the initial letter of each of these three words

explanation.surface: A Welshman begins gilding an English-language Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords often use a typical Welsh name such as Evan, Dai or Ivor to stand for a Welshman.
explanation.definitionFit: Evangel is an old word for the good news of Christianity, or for one of the four books telling it.

clue.text: Fine art style feature over island lake

parts.note: the chin is a facial feature
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over
Is is the abbreviation for island
Lake Erie is one of the Great Lakes

explanation.surface: An art critic describes a painting whose main feature is an island above a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinoiserie is the European decorative style imitating Chinese motifs, popular in the eighteenth century for porcelain and furniture.

clue.text: Clarets do go off, even if they're kept here

definitions.text: Clarets do go off, even if they're kept here

indicators.note: something gone off is spoiled and out of shape, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: eleven letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wine lover laments that red wine can spoil even in a chilled store.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the first part supplies the letters and the full sentence describes the place where the wine is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold storage is a refrigerated place for preserving perishable goods, which the clue pictures holding wine that still spoils.

clue.text: Posh limos regularly scratched here in the US

indicators.note: scratching at regular intervals removes every other letter, leaving the alternate ones

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Upmarket stretch cars keep getting scratched in some American place.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a place in the US named by 'here', which the solver must pin down from the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ohio is one of the fifty American states, so it is a location within the US.

clue.text: Fierce fighting to fluster gasman, according to Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of neighbouring words

parts.note: fluster means rattle, and the gasman is Robert Boyle, of Boyle's law on gases; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to unnerve the man who reads the gas meter, provoking a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: The gasman is not a utility worker but the scientist Boyle, whose law relates the pressure and volume of a gas.
explanation.definitionFit: A battle royal is a free-for-all brawl with many combatants, or any bitterly contested struggle.

clue.text: Lady lodged in pad in Eastbourne after retiring

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the concealed letters are read backwards
the letters are lodged inside the run of words that follows, spanning a word break

parts.note: the letters straddling the end of pad, the word in and the start of Eastbourne

explanation.surface: A woman retires to a flat in Eastbourne, a seaside town favoured by pensioners.
explanation.walkthrough: Eastbourne is a south-coast English resort famous for its retired population, which makes 'retiring' feel like part of the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid is a woman's first name, as in Enid Blyton, and crosswords often clue any female name as lady.

clue.text: Korean rapper, Argentine Marxist and English cook making druggy music?

parts.note: Psy is the South Korean rapper behind Gangnam Style
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary
Delia Smith is a famous English television cook

explanation.surface: An unlikely trio of a pop star, a revolutionary and a TV cook form a band playing trippy music.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: the word covers the whole culture and art of hallucinogenic drugs, music included.
explanation.definitionFit: Psychedelia is the art, music and culture linked to hallucinogens such as LSD, notably the trippy rock of the late 1960s.

clue.text: Poor wee orphans receiving new messages here

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the abbreviation is placed inside the other letters
poor suggests something in a bad state, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: ten letters taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Little orphaned children are sent fresh letters.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as a place: the device where messages are left, described as where they end up.
explanation.definitionFit: An answerphone is a machine that records callers' spoken messages when nobody picks up, so messages are left on it.

clue.text: Star Joey (first seen in Friends) gets opening part in Top Gear

parts.note: the Sun is a star
a joey is a baby kangaroo, or roo

indicators.note: first seen points to the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: the initial letter

explanation.surface: A famous actor who played Joey in Friends lands a role on the BBC motoring show Top Gear.
explanation.walkthrough: Joey suggests Matt LeBlanc's character in Friends, who later presented Top Gear; here it is a young kangaroo, and the definition is a car part.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunroof is a panel in the roof of a car that slides or tilts open, so it is an opening part at the top of a vehicle.

clue.text: Fish dressing that is spicy

indicators.note: dressing is read as clothing or wrapping round, so the fish surrounds the abbreviation

parts.note: fry are young fish
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A sauce for fish is described as hot and spicy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' looks like a salad dressing for the fish, but it means wrapping round.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiery food is hot with chilli or pepper, burning the mouth like fire, which is what spicy describes.

clue.text: Writer Peters appears in court, one associated with Bow

indicators.note: the pen name appears inside the abbreviation, so one sits within the other

parts.note: Ct is the abbreviation for court
Ellis Peters was the pen name of the author of the Cadfael mysteries

explanation.surface: A crime author turns up in court with a link to Bow, an area of London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is a district of east London and Bow Street was a famous magistrates' court, so a courtroom scene feels natural; the capital is a disguise for a violin bow.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellist plays a stringed instrument with a bow, so the bow is the tool most closely tied to the player.

clue.text: Shrewd Conservative always carrying notes

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative

indicators.note: carrying means holding within, so the word for always takes the notes inside

parts.note: ay, also spelt aye, is an old word for always
N for note, twice for the plural

explanation.surface: A shrewd Tory politician never goes anywhere without his speaking notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Ay for always survives in poetry and Scots and is a common crossword stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: Canny is a Scots and northern English word for cautious and astute, especially with money or business.

clue.text: Essential to maintain temperature in bottle

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold, so the bottle holds the abbreviation within it

parts.note: a vial is a small glass bottle
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Instructions say the contents of a bottle must be kept at the right temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Vital and essential are direct synonyms, both meaning absolutely necessary and indispensable.

clue.text: Cold bird of prey that sits on top of chimney

definitions.text: that sits on top of chimney
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the thing that sits there

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
an owl is a hunting bird

explanation.surface: A chilly hawk or owl perches on top of a chimney stack.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird that seems to perch on the chimney is part of the wordplay; the definition is the hood that sits up there.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowl is a hooded metal cover fitted over a chimney pot to stop downdraughts and rain getting in.

clue.text: Carry goods dropped by mendicant

indicators.note: what is dropped by someone is let go, so those letters are taken out of the word

parts.note: a mendicant is a beggar
G for good, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A beggar has to carry whatever goods he lets fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goods' looks like merchandise, but it is G for good, twice; removing GG from BEGGAR leaves BEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something is to hold it up and take it along, the same as carrying it.

clue.text: Smile dutifully when beginning dreary work

parts.note: a grin is a broad smile

indicators.note: beginning picks out only the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the initial letter

explanation.surface: A worker forces a dutiful smile at the start of a tedious shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning dreary' looks like a first letter to take, but 'dreary' belongs to the definition; the letter comes from 'dutifully'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grind is tedious, laborious effort that wears a person down, like the daily routine of a boring job.

clue.text: Family leaves King Lear to grapple with upper-class English complaint

indicators.note: grappling means clutching in a hold, so what remains wraps round the next letters
leaves means departs from, so those letters walk out of the title

parts.note: Shakespeare's tragedy, taken as written
kin are relatives, your family
U is the old label for upper-class usage
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: King Lear's family abandons him to struggle with a posh Englishman's grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear the old king is indeed cast off by his daughters, which makes 'Family leaves King Lear' read as plot summary; removing KIN leaves GLEAR, which then holds U and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Glue ear is a common childhood ailment in which sticky fluid builds up in the middle ear, so it is a medical complaint.

clue.text: Net part integral to wood ark we built

indicators.note: integral to means built into, so the letters are found running inside the following words

parts.note: the letters running from the end of wood through ark and we to the start of built

explanation.surface: Noah describes a vital part of the wooden ark the family built together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net' looks like a fishing net on the ark, but it is short for the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark web is the hidden region of the internet reached only through special software, so it is one section of the Net.

clue.text: Vile muck lorry emptied out

parts.note: muck is dirt or soil

indicators.note: emptying the word removes all its inner letters, keeping only the outside pair

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A filthy truck full of dirt is tipped out.
explanation.walkthrough: This uses an old sense found in Chambers: earthly as base or mean, the opposite of heavenly.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthly in its old sense means base, low and worldly rather than spiritual, so it can stand for vile.

clue.text: Deviating from course around noon, clearly tired

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the swerving word goes round the letter for noon

parts.note: a ship or plane yaws when it swings off its heading
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A sleepy sailor drifts off course at midday.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who keeps opening their mouth wide and gulping air is plainly showing fatigue, the visible sign of being sleepy.

clue.text: Genuine theatrical giant (not British)

indicators.note: not tells the solver to do without the abbreviation inside the brackets

parts.note: Bertolt Brecht, the hugely influential German playwright and director
Br is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A towering stage figure is praised as authentic, not being British.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant' suggests size, but it means a major figure; removing BR from BRECHT leaves ECHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Echt is a German borrowing used in English to mean authentic, real or typical of its kind.

clue.text: Ultraviolet beam exposed section of the eye

parts.note: UV is the standard abbreviation for ultraviolet

indicators.note: exposed means stripped of its covering, so the outer letters are removed and the middle kept

parts.note: the inner letters once the first and last are gone

explanation.surface: An eye is exposed to a damaging ultraviolet ray.
explanation.definitionFit: The uvea is the pigmented middle layer of the eyeball, made up of the iris, ciliary body and choroid.

clue.text: Areas in theatres where one might see Hamilton?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the seating or orchestra areas on the floor of a theatre
second meaning: the service bays beside a motor-racing track, where Lewis Hamilton stops for tyres

explanation.walkthrough: Hamilton is a hit stage musical, so the clue seems to stay in the theatre; the question mark flags the switch to the Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both the sunken floor sections of a playhouse and the trackside garages where racing drivers stop during a Grand Prix.

clue.text: Small tool that extends over a foot

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the thing that covers a foot

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes
a hoe is a garden tool

explanation.surface: A little implement measures slightly longer than twelve inches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extends over a foot' reads as a length of more than twelve inches, but it means covering the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe is footwear that covers the foot, so it is the thing that stretches across it.

clue.text: Fury maybe raging why I hate veg?

indicators.note: raging means wildly out of control, so the following letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: eleven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry child fumes about why they hate vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: Fury looks like anger, matching 'raging', but it is Tyson Fury, the boxing champion; 'maybe' shows he is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyson Fury has held world titles in boxing's top weight division, so he is an example of a fighter in that class.

clue.text: Northern Europeans eschewing loud pubs

indicators.note: eschewing means avoiding or doing without, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: people from Finland
f, forte, is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: Quiet Scandinavian tourists avoid noisy bars.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn is a traditional pub or tavern offering drink and often lodging, so the plural means pubs.

clue.text: When drunk, eats kebab, with case of disorder in tummy

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: nine letters taken as written

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: After a night's drinking someone wolfs a kebab and ends up with an upset stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: A kebab after a night out drinking is a well-known British habit, which makes the scene feel real.
explanation.definitionFit: Breadbasket is humorous slang for the stomach, the place where food such as bread ends up.
